Thank you for submitting your work entitled "Temporal profiling of redox-dependent heterogeneity in single cells" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been evaluated by a Senior Editor and three reviewers, one of whom, Agnieszka Chacinska (Reviewer #1), is a member of our Board of Reviewing Editors. The following individual involved in review of your submission has agreed to reveal their identity: Michel B Toledano (Reviewer #2).

Our decision has been reached after consultation between the reviewers. As you will see from the individual comments, the reviewers appreciated the interesting question and a rich set of high quality data. However, in the current form the manuscript seems to be at the stage that is not sufficiently mature to invite well-defined additions and comments. Summarizing the reviewer’s comments, the paper requires some major shaping based on the three points, to 1) streamline and focus the story, 2) expand some parts experimentally and 3) apply more rigor when drawing the conclusions.

Ad. 1) as suggested in the individual reviews some part may be either omitted or better linked to the rest of the paper, including some additional analyses if required.

Ad. 2) several important issues have been raised. The manuscript definitely requires the clarification in terms of replicative vs. chronological aging, and clarification of the respiratory status of the cells. Furthermore, some of the other aspects should be addressed, e. g. specifying the role of the redox-changing proteins identified in this study. In case, if experimental clarification goes beyond the scope or is technically too challenging, the authors should carefully phrase the conclusions in reference to the point 3).

Given the high potential of the story seen by the reviewers, we would like to encourage the resubmission of the manuscript. To have high chances in eLife, the manuscript must be properly revised in terms of all three points mentioned above, including new experimental data. The revised version of the manuscript will likely be evaluated by the same reviewers who are willing to have another look.

Reviewer #1:

This is an interesting resource paper that identifies a phenotypic variability in the yeast population in terms of the cellular redox state of glutathione. The authors used an in vivo redox sensor to isolate different populations of cells being with a more oxidized or more reduced status. The populations have been characterized for their fitness and systematically analyzed to identify the differences in the abundance of proteins and in transcriptomics.

The paper is rich in data centered around a really interesting question. It gives a first systemic glance on the molecular changes underlying the phenomenon of variability in redox states of the cells and their dynamics in time and during cell division. The data are slightly descriptive, but this is a resource paper.

The following points should be taken under considerations to revise the work:

- The three proteins identified in the study based on their enrichment in the reduced or oxidized state were functionally examined and concluded to take part in dynamic processes that shape the redox potential of the cell. Hsp30 was in fact implicated earlier. Having established such exciting technology the authors are able to ask more precise questions on which stage these proteins act. Does their absence modify the dynamics of cellular redox changes in the entire population by changing the redox state values of both population groups? Do they affect a bimodal behavior observed in the cell population, i.e. by modifying the number of reduced vs oxidized cells? Does their absence change the ability to enter into the irreversible phase of the oxidized state, or perhaps the daughters of old oxidized mothers are less efficiently recovering into a reduced state?

- There are plenty of examples, in this study and literature, that the transcriptomics and proteomics frequently do not agree perfectly well. It would interesting to undertake more systematic analyses to see the extent of correlations.

- This is somewhat not surprising that the daughter cell inherits the redox status, also the oxidized status, from the mother. An interesting and surprising thing is however that some daughter cells may retain the ability to recover as briefly mentioned at the end of the Results section. This part is somehow slightly underdeveloped in the manuscript. Could the authors develop this part further?

- The authors should avoid bold statements. As already mentioned, the results are largely of correlative nature, and causes and consequences are unclear. For example, I do not see the basis for the following statement: "…we suggest that the redox status, rather than cell age, is a critical determinant of cellular growth and division properties". The text should be carefully evaluated to avoid the statements that do not have a source in literature or in the authors data.

Reviewer #2:

In this paper, Reichmann and colleagues measured the redox state of the GSH redox probe Grx1-roGFP2 in the cytosol of yeast cells during chronological aging, and found that the probe oxidized overtime. They could then distinguish two subpopulations, one that remained reduced, but diminished during aging, and the other more oxidized that increased. They sorted these two populations by FACS, and inspected their growth phenotype, their transcriptome and proteome. They identified 4 proteins that are differently expressed in the two subpopulations, and tested their influence on the redox state of roGFP2 by the effect of the corresponding gene deletions. They conclude on the presence of a redox heterogeneity within the same cell population that can be transmitted to daughter cells.

This is an interesting paper that addresses a wild unexplored question of possible redox heterogeneity within a yeast population, and provides an intriguing answer to as the basis of the observed heterogeneity, and possible role of a few selected protein in redox control/aging. The enormous amount of work presented appears very rigorously performed.

There is, however, a concern regarding the interpretation of the data of Figure 4, on which the paper's conclusion is built up. Authors distinguished within a yeast population undergoing chronological aging two subpopulations with a different roGFP2 redox state. Upon inspection of these populations, they found that the reduced one had very few bud scars (< 1), and the oxidized one 3-4.5 more scars: the question is whether the two subpopulations differ by their replicative aging status, with those remaining reduced being newly born daughter cells, and those that oxidize being mother cells, which already underwent a few division, which would be consistent with their growth phenotype, and with the notion that cells oxidize Grx1-roGFP2 during replicative aging, when grown in a respiratory medium (Kniess and Mayer, 2016)? If this the case would collapse the authors' claim that the differences of the two subpopulations are redox, intrinsically, and not age-dependent.

There are a few other points that must be addressed, as described below.

1) Authors must evaluate the possible difference in replicative aging status between the two cells subpopulations: At best, they could sort old and young cells, based on the number of budscars, as done by Kniess and Mayer, and evaluate the redox state of their cytosol during chronological aging, or simultaneously sort cells according to their redox state and budscar status.

2) Table 1 indicate the presence of 30% of reduced cell undergoing budding: It would seem however that chronological aging is the survival of a post-replicative stationary culture: please comment.

3) The mitochondrial status (respiration) should also be established within the two subpopulations.

4) Figure 3C: it is surprising to see that the increase in oxidation during aging gives oxidation values (ratio 405/488) higher than the one measured with diamide (Figure 1D). Please, comment. At best, data should be displayed here using OxD, rather than ratios of fluorescence.

5) The values of OxD measured in the cytosol are much higher than published ones using the same probe (Kojer et al., 2012): 0.3 in Wt cytosol (Figure 2A) vs. 0.1. These values are also different in the different figures, which makes the comparison with mutants difficult. In Figure 6E and 7D values in Wt are < 0.1 and those of mutant similar to Wt in 2A. The total probe oxidation of ddh1D at 96 h is very surprising: are these cells dying? Please comment.

6) The first figures of the paper do not appear really informative and might distract/confuse the reader: Figure 1 displays published data (Kojer et al., 2012). Figure 2 does not provide any data that fit the current story, and use of Glr1 in 3 is not informative because it is known that Glr has a dominant function in reducing glutathione.

Reviewer #3:

In their manuscript "Temporal profiling of redox-dependent heterogeneity in single cells" Radzinski et al. present a method to track the redox state of individual cells using a combination of genetically encoded fluorescent redox probes and FACS. Using this methodology, they discover a bi-modal distribution of reduced and oxidized yeast cells in a chronologically aging population. They then proceed to analyze these 2 subpopulations using proteomics and transcriptomics and follow up on some of their findings, identifying Hsp30, Dhh1 and Pnc1 as potential regulators of the cellular redox homeostasis.

The authors present an impressive amount of data and overall, their results suggest that current assumptions about the redox state in aging cells are too simplistic and need to be revised. A model that assumes a simultaneous and uniform decrease in the redox state in all cells of an aging population must be dismissed. And even when considering reproductive aging, the authors could show that daughters can "inherit" the oxidation state of their mothers.

However, some of their data analyses do not seem very productive, in particular some of the STRING-based interaction networks and the functional enrichment. A removal of parts of these analyses would probably not affect their overall conclusions. Should they decide to keep these analyses, they need to justify them and describe these analyses in more detail: What were the criteria chosen by the authors to identify an interaction in the interaction networks? What does it e.g. mean if "Hsp30 is connected to Dhh1"? Is it justified to have proteins that were up-regulated in both reduced and oxidized sub-populations in the very same interaction network? What does it mean, if proteins that "interact" are upregulated under diametrically opposed conditions? How were functions defined for the functional enrichment analyses?

The authors should also submit their proteomics and transcriptomics data to appropriate repositories (e.g. the EMBL PRIDE archive, ArrayExpress, or GEO).

Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "Temporal profiling of redox-dependent heterogeneity in single cells" for further consideration at eLife. Your revised article has been favorably evaluated by Didier Stainier (Senior Editor) and three reviewers, one of whom is a member of our Board of Reviewing Editors.

The reviewers agree that the author did a great job. The reviewers were in fact impressed by the amount and quality of the majority of data. Overall the manuscript is rich in interesting and valuable conclusions. However, there are still some questions raised that require text clarification and discussion. These points are appended below and should be carefully and fully addressed and some shortcomings and limitations should be acknowledged.

We would like to draw your attention to the issue of the oxidation data (the point 2 of reviewer 2). These data should be provided in a full version, and not only as ratios.

Reviewer #2:

1) The heterogeneity in probe oxidation the authors saw during chronologic aging might have been the result of differences in replicative aging, and not just of cellular heterogeneity; in other words, roGFP oxidation distinguished within an asynchronous chronologically aging cell culture old mother from young daughter cells.

Authors did a terrific job in isolating old mother cells, by genetic enrichment that select against young daughter cells, and now can establish correlations between replicative, chronologic life span and probe oxidation (Figure 5).

The 24 h data clearly indicates that roGFP oxidation follows RLS. Of the 72-h data, there is a superposition of RLS and CLS: since only mother cells are selected, those that still have a sufficient replicative potential, will therefore inexorably age replicatively, which is what shows Figure 5E, and therefore oxidize (according to the 24 h data). The oxidation shift observed in old cells at 72 h, relative to 24 h might be a consequence of CLS of old, already oxidized cells. Probe oxidation during chronologic aging is anyhow nicely shown in Figure 2.

In conclusion, the redox heterogeneity of a bulk cell culture must be, at least in a large part, contributed to by differences in replicative aging, a conclusion which should be applied to the all study: it is indeed delusive to consider that the 3% reduced cells within 72 h grown old mother cells (Figure 5E) to be representative of the initial reduced and oxidized population used for proteomics and transcriptomics: this might require a bit of reorganization of the paper. Another issue raised by these new data: they are surprisingly totally discrepant with those of Kniess and Mayer (2016), who found a reduction of roGFP2-Grx1 during replicative aging in fermentative medium): authors should definitely address this discrepancy.

2) In the previous evaluation, I asked: "Figure 3C: it is surprising to see that the increase in oxidation during aging gives oxidation values (ratio 405/488) higher than the one measured with diamide (Figure 1D). Please, comment. At best, data should be displayed here using OxD, rather than ratios of fluorescence". Authors nicely introduced OxD values, which is understood as not fitting analyses of heterogeneous cell populations. However, they did not answer the first question: at best, in Figure 2C (former 3C), authors should show the abundance/405/488 ratio graphs for the control DTT and diamide, since they must have been done to calculate the OxDs of Figure 2A.

Another concern I had: "The total probe oxidation of ddh1D at 96 h is very surprising: are these cells dying? Please comment". This tremendous oxidation, equal to the one seen with the diamide control, is extremely surprising. Accordingly, to convince readers, and also avoid any experimental caveats, it seems appropriate to directly measure the levels of GSH and GSSG in whole cells by enzymatic assay, in the same conditions as those of figure 2A (at least time 0 and 72 h) and Figure 7A. It should be acknowledged that this is not the best control, but the only available: whole cells monitoring of GSH and GSSG is biased by the sequestration of GSSG in the vacuole, therefore giving higher levels of GSSG than those actually present in the cytosol (Morgan et al., 2013).

results.result: The authors developed a flow cytometry-based methodology using the Grx1-roGFP2 redox sensor to measure and sort yeast cells based on their redox status at single-cell resolution in the cytosol, mitochondria, and peroxisomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C15, C24-C28 establish the methodology development and validation. The alternating fluorescence peaks at 405/488 nm (C25, C26) with distinct linear fits (R²=0.99 and 0.97) provide strong quantitative evidence. The method's applicability to organelle-specific sensors (C28) and ability to create gates for sorting (C27) demonstrate technical robustness. The methodology is well-characterized with appropriate controls.

results.result: Chronologically aging yeast cells exhibit a bi-modal distribution of redox status, with cells transitioning from reduced to oxidized states over time, while mitochondrial oxidation shows greater robustness than cytosolic oxidation.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C32-C34 demonstrate the bi-modal distribution with clear temporal dynamics. The largest shift occurs at 48 hr (C34), supported by Figure 2C. The comparison between cytosolic and mitochondrial oxidation (C29-C31) provides compartment-specific insights. However, the interpretation of 'robustness' (C31) is somewhat speculative and would benefit from mechanistic investigation.

results.result: Reduced and oxidized yeast subpopulations display distinct growth characteristics, with reduced cells showing faster doubling times, fewer bud scars, and higher budding rates compared to oxidized cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C41 provide converging evidence from multiple phenotypic assays. The quantitative differences in minimal doubling time (C36), bud scars (3-4.5× more in oxidized, C39), and budding rates (~30% in reduced vs. lower in oxidized, C40) are well-documented. The interpretation that oxidized cells have impaired division rather than inability to enter log phase (C37) is supported by similar lag phases. Statistical significance is mentioned but p-values are not always provided.

results.result: Oxidized cells exhibit a metabolic shift from oxidative phosphorylation to glycolysis, with 1.8-2 fold lower oxygen consumption rate and 2-2.8 fold higher extracellular acidification rate compared to reduced cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C43 provide quantitative Seahorse assay data with clear fold-changes. The interpretation as a Warburg-like effect (C44) is reasonable given the OCR/ECAR patterns, though the comparison to cancer metabolism could be more cautiously stated. Three biological replicates were analyzed (mentioned in text), providing adequate statistical power. The correlation with growth (C45) is logical but remains correlative.

results.result: Using the Mother Enrichment Program, the authors demonstrate that cellular oxidation correlates strongly but not absolutely with replicative aging (bud scar count), and that chronological aging also contributes to oxidation independent of division events.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C54 use the Mother Enrichment Program to separate replicative from chronological aging effects. The quantitative data (87.8% oxidized in high bud scar at 24h, C47; 36.4% vs 6.5% oxidized in low bud scar at late vs early growth, C50) support the dual contribution model. The observation of 'eternally reduced' highly divided cells (C48, C52) is important but represents a small minority. The interpretation distinguishes correlation from causation appropriately.

results.result: Proteomic analysis identified 3389 proteins, with 1019 consistently detected across subpopulations. Protein expression profiles cluster by redox status rather than age, with reduced cells enriched for energy production and mitochondrial proteins, while oxidized cells show enrichment for protein folding and redox homeostasis proteins.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C64 describe comprehensive proteomic analysis with appropriate bioinformatics. The clustering by redox status rather than age (C58-C59) is a key finding supported by Figure 6A. Functional enrichment analysis (C60, C62) is appropriate, though the statistical thresholds (FDR=0.05, fold change >2) are reasonable. The interpretation connecting proteome to phenotype (C61) is logical. Three biological replicates provide adequate statistical power.

results.result: Comparative proteomic analysis identified differentially expressed proteins between reduced and oxidized populations, including stress response proteins (Hsp30, Dhh1) upregulated in reduced cells and stress-induced proteins (Gre1, Sro9, Hsp150, Tsa2) upregulated in oxidized cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C17, C65-C71 identify specific differentially expressed proteins with statistical support (199 proteins at 48h, 149 at 72h, C63-C64). The observation of ribosomal protein upregulation in oxidized cells (C66) is interesting, though the interpretation of 'non-functional' ribosomes (C67) is speculative. The 'first line of defense' hypothesis (C71) for stress granule proteins is reasonable but requires functional validation beyond correlation.

results.result: Deletion analysis of candidate proteins revealed that Δdhh1 and Δhsp30 show significantly increased oxidation compared to wild-type, while Δpnc1 shows decreased oxidation. These deletions also affect cellular morphology and growth, with Δdhh1 showing severe phenotypes including enlarged vacuoles and growth arrest.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C83 provide genetic validation of proteomic findings. The oxidation phenotypes are quantified (C72, C75) with statistical testing mentioned. The severe Δdhh1 phenotype (C77-C79) complicates interpretation of its redox role (C144), as oxidation may be secondary to growth defects. The morphological observations (C79, C81-C82) are descriptive but lack quantification. The conclusion that these proteins affect redox homeostasis (C73, C76) is supported but mechanistic details are lacking.

results.result: Analysis of redox distribution in deletion strains reveals distinct patterns: Δtsa2 resembles wild-type, Δdhh1 shows early oxidation and collapse, Δpnc1 remains reduced, and Δhsp30 displays a unique stable bimodal distribution. Organelle-specific analysis shows Hsp30 affects mitochondrial but not peroxisomal redox distribution.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C92 characterize redox distributions in deletion strains. The bimodal distribution in Δhsp30 (C87, C139) is a striking phenotype supported by Figure 7F. The organelle-specific effects (C88, C90-C91) provide spatial resolution, though the speculation about redox synchronization (C89) requires further investigation. The interpretation of distinct modes of redox regulation (C92) is reasonable but remains largely descriptive without mechanistic insight.

results.result: Transcriptomic analysis identified ~5000 genes in each subpopulation, with global changes clustering by redox status rather than age. Reduced cells show upregulation of carbon metabolism, TCA cycle, and lipid biosynthesis genes. While global correlation exists between transcriptome and proteome, specific examples of uncoupling were observed, notably for Hsp30 and Yro2.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C101 describe transcriptomic analysis with appropriate statistical thresholds (FDR<0.05, fold change ≥2). The clustering by redox status (C94) parallels proteomic findings. The observation of mRNA-protein uncoupling (C98, C100) is important, particularly for Hsp30 where mRNA is high in oxidized but protein is high in reduced cells. The speculation about differential turnover (C101) is reasonable but requires validation. The discrepancy between proteome and transcriptome for peroxisomal proteins (C96-C97) is well-explained by abundance limitations.

results.result: Hsp30 shows antagonistic regulation at mRNA and protein levels, with high mRNA in oxidized cells but high protein in reduced cells. Deletion of Hsp30 increases cellular oxidation and creates a unique bimodal redox distribution, suggesting Hsp30 enhances redox heterogeneity and may serve as a 'redox keeper'.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C140 focus on Hsp30 as a key regulator. The mRNA-protein discordance (C133, C136) is well-documented. The deletion phenotype (C134, C139) provides functional evidence. The speculation about impaired protein turnover (C136-C138) is reasonable but lacks direct measurement of protein stability or translation rates. The 'redox keeper' concept is supported by the deletion phenotype but the mechanism remains unclear. The bimodal distribution in Δhsp30 (C139-C140) is intriguing but interpretation requires further investigation.

results.result: Dhh1, a stress granule-associated RNA helicase, is upregulated in reduced cells and its deletion leads to elevated oxidation, growth arrest, and cellular collapse. Other stress granule-associated proteins show similar upregulation in reduced cells, with protein but not transcript changes suggesting post-transcriptional regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C141-C147 identify Dhh1 as important for redox homeostasis, but the severe pleiotropic phenotype of Δdhh1 (C143, C77-C79) makes it difficult to determine if oxidation is a primary or secondary effect (C144). The observation that other stress granule proteins are upregulated in reduced cells (C145) without transcript changes (C147) is interesting, but the speculation about p-body migration (C146) lacks direct evidence. The role of Dhh1 in redox regulation requires more targeted experiments to separate direct from indirect effects.

results.result: Pnc1, a nicotinamidase upregulated in oxidized cells, shows opposite effects when deleted: Δpnc1 cells are more reduced than wild-type. The authors propose Pnc1 links reduced stress, nicotinamide accumulation, and decreased cell viability through Sir2 inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C148-C149 show Pnc1 upregulation in oxidized cells and a more reduced phenotype upon deletion, which is paradoxical but well-documented. The connection to Sir2 and lifespan (C150) is supported by prior literature. The proposed model (C151) linking Pnc1 to redox stress and viability is speculative but builds on established knowledge. However, the mechanism by which Pnc1 deletion leads to reducing stress requires further investigation, and the model remains largely correlative.

results.result: Time-lapse imaging reveals that cells can self-correct their oxidation status through fluctuations, but only below a threshold of approximately OxD* 0.7 (70% of maximal oxidation). Once cells cross this threshold, they cannot recover and maintain high oxidation until death.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C109, C152-C154 describe single-cell dynamics over 12 hours. The identification of an oxidation threshold at ~0.7 OxD* (C106, C154) is a key finding supported by Figure 9. The observation that cells can fluctuate below but not above this threshold (C105, C107-C108) suggests a bistable system. However, the sample size (>30 cells) is relatively small for establishing a precise threshold value. The mechanism underlying this threshold behavior is not explored and represents an important area for future work.

results.result: Mother and daughter cells have identical oxidation levels during and immediately after budding, regardless of the mother's initial oxidation state. Some daughter cells can self-correct their inherited oxidation within an hour after separation, suggesting the oxidized state inheritance is a regulated mechanism rather than simple diffusion.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C114, C155-C156 demonstrate mother-daughter oxidation inheritance using time-lapse imaging (Figure 10). The observation of identical OxD* values during budding (C111) is clear. The ability of some daughters to self-correct (C113) is important but the frequency and determinants of this correction are not quantified. The interpretation that inheritance is regulated rather than diffusive (C156) is reasonable given the time scale (several hours) exceeds duplication time, but direct evidence for a regulatory mechanism is lacking. The sample size for budding events is not specified.

results.result: The study identifies a new type of glutathione-dependent heterogeneity in genetically identical yeast cells, where redox status contributes to cellular growth and division properties. The transition from reduced to oxidized status appears to be a threshold-based phenomenon leading to distinct subpopulations with different growth potential and biochemical profiles.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C16, C18-C19, C119-C121 synthesize the major findings. The identification of redox-dependent heterogeneity (C2, C119) is well-supported by the bi-modal distributions, differential growth, and distinct molecular profiles. The claim that redox status 'contributes to' rather than 'determines' cellular properties (C120) is appropriately cautious. The threshold-based model (C121) is supported by the imaging data but is presented as speculation. The study successfully demonstrates correlation between redox status and multiple cellular phenotypes, though causality is not definitively established.

results.result: Three proteins—Hsp30, Dhh1, and Pnc1—are proposed as 'first line of defense' proteins in redox homeostasis based on their differential expression and effects on basal oxidation levels when deleted.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C17, C71, C73, C76, C92 propose these three proteins as key redox regulators. While the proteomic data (differential expression) and genetic data (deletion phenotypes) are solid, the 'first line of defense' designation (C6, C71) is speculative. For Dhh1, the severe pleiotropic effects make it difficult to assess its direct role in redox regulation. For Hsp30, the mechanism is unclear despite the clear phenotype. For Pnc1, the paradoxical effect (upregulated in oxidized, but deletion causes reduction) requires mechanistic explanation. The claim would be strengthened by rescue experiments, direct measurement of antioxidant activity, or demonstration that these proteins respond to oxidative stress before other markers.

results.result: Background and context: Cellular redox status affects diverse functions, existing methods for measuring redox status have limitations, and cell-to-cell heterogeneity in genetically identical populations is well-established, but redox heterogeneity within synchronized cells had not been explored.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C7-C14, C22-C23, C115-C118 provide literature context. These are appropriately cited general knowledge claims that establish the rationale for the study. The identification of a gap in knowledge (C14) regarding redox heterogeneity in synchronized cells is accurate and motivates the work. The limitations of existing methods (C10-C11) justify the methodological development.

results.result: Background on specific proteins and methods: roGFP probes are established tools, Hsp30 is a stress-induced membrane protein, Dhh1 is a stress granule helicase, and Pnc1 affects Sir2 activity and lifespan.
results.evaluation: Claims C123, C128-C132, C142, C150 provide background on tools and proteins studied. These are well-cited claims from prior literature that provide context for interpreting the current results. The speculation about future applications (C128-C129) is reasonable but represents potential rather than demonstrated utility.

results.result: Summary claims about thresholds and inheritance: There is a threshold above which cells cannot maintain redox homeostasis, and mother cells pass oxidized states to daughters, with maternal influence playing a central role in daughter cell oxidative stress.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C21, C110, C114 summarize key findings about thresholds and inheritance. These are supported by the imaging data (Figures 9-10) and integrate well with the other results. The citation to prior work on maternal age effects (C110) provides appropriate context.
